nameStory: The Armyworm Moth gets its dramatic name from the behavior of its caterpillars, which move across fields in massive groups like a marching army. These caterpillar 'armies' travel from field to field in organized lines, often devastating crops in their path. It's also called the white-speck moth because of a distinctive white spot on each forewing.
description: The Armyworm Moth is a medium-sized brown moth in the cutworm family, most active at night when it's drawn to lights. The adult moths have mottled brown wings that help them blend in during the day when they rest on tree bark or fence posts. While the moths themselves are fairly inconspicuous, their caterpillars are notorious agricultural pests that can strip entire fields bare. These moths are remarkable travelers, migrating north in spring and south in fall across much of North America.

idTips.label: White forewing spot
idTips.description: Look for a distinctive white or pale yellow spot in the center of each brown forewing - this is the 'white speck' that gives the moth one of its common names

idTips.label: Mottled brown coloring
idTips.description: Wings have a streaky, mottled brown pattern that feels rough to the touch, helping the moth blend perfectly against tree bark when resting

idTips.label: Medium size
idTips.description: About the size of your thumb when wings are spread, smaller than the large sphinx moths but bigger than many of the tiny moths that swarm porch lights

idTips.label: Night activity
idTips.description: Most active after dark and strongly attracted to artificial lights - you'll often find them clinging to lit windows or porch lights in the morning

idTips.label: Tent-like resting pose
idTips.description: During the day, rests with wings folded in a triangular, tent-like shape against vertical surfaces like tree trunks or building walls

habitat: Armyworm Moths are found throughout New England in open areas where grasses grow, including agricultural fields, meadows, prairies, and suburban lawns. They prefer areas with abundant grasses and crops like corn, wheat, and hay, which their caterpillars feed on. You'll often encounter the adults around outdoor lights in rural and suburban areas during their migration periods.

seasonality.spring: Adults arrive from southern regions during spring migration, appearing at lights and beginning to mate and lay eggs in grassy areas.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period with adults most commonly seen at night lights, and caterpillars may be found marching in groups across fields and lawns during outbreak years.
seasonality.fall: Adults prepare for southern migration, with numbers often increasing at lights before they begin their journey south for winter.
seasonality.winter: Not present in New England - the species migrates south to warmer regions where it can survive freezing temperatures.

funFact: Armyworm Moths have superhero-level hearing that helps them dodge hungry bats in the dark - they can detect the ultrasonic calls bats use for hunting and will instantly dive or zigzag to escape being caught mid-flight!
confusionNotes: Many brown moths look similar at first glance, but the white spot on each forewing is your best clue - most other brown noctuids have different marking patterns. If you can't see the white spot clearly, remember that armyworm moths are often more numerous than other species during migration periods.
contextualKnowledge: This moth is actually in the genus Mythimna according to current scientific classification, though you may still see it listed under the older name Pseudaletia in some field guides. Despite being called an 'armyworm,' the problematic stage is actually the caterpillar, not the adult moth, which is a harmless pollinator.
compareHints: Since this is the only Pseudaletia species in our dataset for New England, compare it with other common brown moths in the cutworm family (Noctuidae). Unlike many of its nocturid relatives, the Armyworm Moth has that distinctive white forewing spot and shows strong migratory behavior rather than overwintering locally. Most similar brown moths lack the prominent white marking and don't show the same seasonal abundance patterns.
